results.summary: TRI-1 Euler is a GF16 dot-product engine that computes a 4-element dot product using four parallel GF16 multipliers and a three-adder reduction tree. It is part of a larger Trinity TRI-NET family and is described as an e-engine SKU with support for multiple numeric formats, quantizers, and power modules. The default configuration computes dot4([1,2,3,4],[1,2,3,4]) = 30.0, observable as 0x47C0 on the output pins after reset. No external hardware is required, but the documentation is largely promotional and does not substantiate many of the claimed features.

This design implements a 5-bit LFSR-based pseudo-random number generator with key-based logic locking, where an incorrect 2-bit key poisons the feedback path and drains the register to zero. A sampled value is reduced modulo a user-supplied maximum and displayed as the last decimal digit on a 7-segment display. The design requires an active-high 7-segment display, a clock source, and switches or buttons for the maximum value, key bits, and sample control. It is a compact demonstration of logic locking applied to an LFSR, with the locking mechanism being the notable feature.

This SystemVerilog design performs grayscale conversion, Sobel edge detection, and thresholding on pixel data received over an SPI interface. Processing modes are selected via input pins, and an internal LFSR can optionally supply test pixels instead of external SPI data. The design requires an external SPI master such as a Raspberry Pi to send pixel data, and the processed result appears on a single output pin. The documentation is brief but includes a block diagram and pin-level usage details, though the thresholding and LFSR behavior are only lightly described.

PulseMon8 is an 8-bit pulse monitor that counts rising edges on an external signal sampled by the Tiny Tapeout clock, with edge detection, compare-match, freeze-on-match, and overflow status outputs. Counting is controlled by enable and clear inputs, and an 8-bit comparison value can be set to trigger match and freeze behavior. The design requires no custom external hardware and can be tested on a demoboard using switches, buttons, or a function generator, though mechanical buttons may bounce and produce spurious edges. The documentation is thorough and includes step-by-step test procedures for counting, comparison, freezing, and overflow.

This project is described as an Advent of Code day-1 style position coprocessor implemented in Hardcaml with a byte-serial Tiny Tapeout wrapper, but the provided documentation instead describes a 640x480 VGA animation of a bouncing backpack mascot bitmap. The VGA output drives a TinyVGA PMOD, and input pins toggle tiling and palette rotation effects. The design requires a TinyVGA PMOD or equivalent VGA DAC and a VGA monitor, and needs a ~25.175 MHz clock. There is a clear mismatch between the title and the documentation, so the actual function of the submitted design is ambiguous.

This design implements a Hamming(7,4) error-correcting code system that can encode 4-bit data into a 7-bit codeword and decode a received codeword while detecting and correcting a single-bit error. A MODE input selects between encoding and decoding, and an error flag output indicates when a correctable error was detected. No external hardware is required beyond input switches and LEDs to observe the encoded or corrected output. The documentation is very short and does not describe the internal implementation or provide test vectors.

This design continuously transmits a looping serial bit stream and detects a hardcoded 9-bit birthday pattern within it, counting hits per second and displaying the count on two 7-segment digits. Transmission is enabled by an active-low input, and a valid pulse indicates when the hit count is updated each second. The design requires external 7-segment displays for the tens and units digits, and no other custom hardware. The documentation is detailed and includes step-by-step test instructions, though the design is essentially a fixed-pattern detector with limited configurability.

This project is titled harveywilly and described only as a tiny tapeout demo, with pin names matching the Tiny VGA PMOD standard. The documentation consists of the phrases 'Ask Pat' and 'Use the code', providing no explanation of what the design does or how it works. The pinout suggests a VGA output design, but no functional details are given. There is essentially no usable documentation for this project.

This project implements a number guessing game in hardware where a 4-bit LFSR generates a pseudo-random number between 1 and 15, and the user has three attempts to guess it. After each guess, outputs indicate whether the correct number is higher, lower, or correct, and the remaining attempts are shown. A new game is started by pulsing an input, and guesses are submitted by pulsing a verify input. No external hardware is required beyond LEDs or a logic analyzer, and the design originates from an IEEE OpenSilicon bootcamp.

This design implements a 2-bit PWM generator using a free-running 2-bit counter, with the duty cycle selected by two reference input bits to produce 0%, 25%, 50%, or 75% output. The PWM output can drive an LED, an RC low-pass filter for analog voltage generation, or a motor driver. Two additional state input bits are connected internally but unused in the current logic. The documentation is clear and includes a duty-cycle table and test steps, and the design is a simple educational PWM example.
